How to Use This Book

This book covers the whole of Section B of MTE 4101 (the programmable logic controller part, taught by Priyo Sir) so that it can be prepared without opening the slides. Every chapter follows the same order:

  1. Theory: everything on the lecture slides, rewritten as exam-ready paragraphs, tables and point lists, with the textbook (W. Bolton, Programmable Logic Controllers, 4th ed.) used where the slides are only pictures or are silent.
  2. Programs: every ladder diagram is drawn rung by rung with rung numbers and Siemens addresses (I0.0, Q0.0, M0.0, T1, C1, MW10), with instruction lists, SFCs, function block diagrams and timing charts where they are asked.
  3. Solved past questions: every Section B question of the 2022, 2023 and 2024 term finals, quoted word for word, answered at the length the marks call for.
  4. Checking: every program in the book was run in a small scan-cycle simulator (the same rung description that draws the ladder); the timing charts of the answers are simulation results, and the checks are quoted under each answer.

Trend analysis: what is repeatedly asked
Program design dominates: about two-thirds of the marks ask for a ladder program (timers, counters, shift registers, data handling), and 2024 set two 20-mark complete-machine designs that combine timers, counters, shift registers, data handling and jumps. Asked in all three years: internal/battery-backed relays (Ch. 4), shift registers (Ch. 8), data handling (Ch. 9). Asked in two years: ladder basics and scanning (identical question 2022/2023), IL and SFC, subroutines, timers, counters, and safety/fault finding (2023 and 2024). Prepare Ch. 6, 8 and 9 (design) and Ch. 4 first; learn the theory of Ch. 2, 3 and 10 for the short questions.

Appendix: Formula Sheet, Instruction Summary and Answer Key

1. PLC Hardware, Internal Architecture and I/O Wiring ★★★

1.1 What a PLC Is

Definition (lecture)
A programmable logic controller (PLC) is a user-friendly, microprocessor-based special-purpose computer, made of hardware and software, designed to control the operation of industrial equipment and processes. Its program is stored in memory and can be easily programmed and reprogrammed. It reads input devices (switches, sensors), executes logic, timing, counting, sequencing and arithmetic instructions, and switches output devices (motors, valves, lamps).

A controller is the unit of a control system that generates control signals so that the actual value of a variable follows the desired value; its task may be to control a sequence of events, to hold a variable constant, or to make it follow a prescribed change. The PLC replaced hard-wired relay panels because it is:

  • Flexible — changing the control logic means editing the program, not rewiring the panel;
  • Reliable and rugged — no moving contacts in the logic; built for electrical noise, vibration, temperature and humidity;
  • Compact and cheap — one small unit replaces hundreds of relays, timers and counters; falling microprocessor cost keeps widening its use;
  • Easy to program and fault-find — ladder language looks like relay circuits, and the on-line monitor shows which contacts are closed;
  • Communicative — it can exchange data with other PLCs, HMIs, SCADA and computers.

The lecture examples use the Siemens LOGO! (e.g. 8 digital inputs, 4 relay outputs, 24 V or 230 V supply) and the Siemens S7-1200 CPU 1215C DC/DC/Relay (24 V d.c. supply, 14 d.c. inputs I0.0–I1.5, 10 relay outputs Q0.0–Q1.1, 8 KB of bit memory M0.0–M8191.7). Siemens addressing (I0.0, Q0.0, M0.0, T1, C1, MW10) is used throughout this book; TIA Portal writes the same addresses with a % sign (%I0.0, %Q0.0). Where a question uses Mitsubishi addresses (X400 inputs, Y430 outputs, M100 auxiliary relays) they are kept.

1.2 Main Functional Blocks

BlockFunction (lecture)
Power supply moduleConverts the 120/230 V a.c. line to the low d.c. voltages used inside: typically 24 V d.c. for the I/O modules and 5 V d.c. for the processor, using rectifier and regulator circuits. It is an integral part of the PLC.
Input module (interface)Connects push buttons, limit switches, sensors, potentiometers and pressure switches. It converts the field signal level (e.g. 24 V d.c. or 230 V a.c.) to the low logic level the CPU uses, and isolates it. Digital inputs become 0/1 signals; analog inputs (0–10 V, 4–20 mA from temperature or pressure transmitters) are converted to integers by an ADC.
Central processing unit (CPU)The “brain”: it receives the input states, executes the user program, makes the control decisions, performs arithmetic and data manipulation, and delivers the output signals. It also handles communication with a PC, remote I/O, other PLCs and peripherals.
MemorySystem (executive) memory holds the operating system; user memory holds the program and the data (image tables, timers, counters, internal relays, registers).
Output moduleAmplifies the low-level logic signals from the CPU and switches the final control elements: contactor coils, solenoid valves, lamps. Relay, transistor or triac outputs are used.
Communications interfaceReceives and transmits data on networks to and from remote PLCs; handles device verification, data acquisition, synchronisation between user applications and connection management.
Programming device / softwareA PC (or handheld programmer) with the vendor software (e.g. TIA Portal) used to create the project, configure the hardware, write, download, monitor and test the program. The PLC itself runs an operating system plus the user program.

1.3 Internal Architecture and Buses

The CPU contains the microprocessor, memory and I/O circuitry. A clock (typically 1–8 MHz in small PLCs, much faster in modern ones) sets the operating speed and synchronises all parts. Inside the microprocessor are:

  1. an arithmetic and logic unit (ALU) — data manipulation, addition and subtraction, and the logic operations AND, OR, NOT and EXCLUSIVE-OR;
  2. registers — fast memory locations that hold information used during program execution (accumulator, status word);
  3. a control unit — times and sequences the operations.

A bus is a set of parallel conductors (PCB tracks or ribbon cable) along which binary signals travel. Each bus carries one kind of information:

BusCarriesDirection
Data busThe data words being read or written (e.g. 8, 16 or 32 bits at a time) between CPU, memory and I/O unit.Two-way
Address busThe address of the memory location or I/O port the CPU wants to access. With nnn address lines, 2n2^n2n locations can be addressed (16 lines → 65 536).One-way, from CPU
Control busTiming and control signals: read/write, clock, interrupt, reset, chip select.From CPU (and status back)
System (I/O) busCommunication between the I/O unit and the input/output ports (channels).Two-way

Memory elements. The system ROM holds the permanent operating system and fixed data; the user-program RAM holds the program; the data RAM holds the input/output image tables, timer and counter values and other variables. RAM is volatile, so a battery (or a capacitor, or flash/EEPROM in modern PLCs) keeps the program and retentive data when power is off. EPROM/EEPROM/flash give non-volatile program storage that can be reprogrammed.

I/O channels. On the input side each channel passes through an opto-coupler (isolation from field voltage spikes) and a buffer. On the output side the CPU writes to a latch, which holds the value until the next update, and a driver interface and drivers (relays, transistors or triacs) switch the load.

1.4 Memory Organization (lecture)

AreaContentsExample
System (executive) memoryManufacturer firmware in ROM/flash: scanning, I/O update, communication, diagnostics. Not changeable by the user.—
User program memoryThe ladder/IL program; flash/EEPROM or battery-backed RAM; reprogrammable in the field.OB1, FC1
Input image table (I)ON/OFF state of every physical input, copied at the start of each scan and held constant during the scan.I0.3 = 1
Output image table (Q)States decided by the program, copied to the physical outputs at the end of the scan.Q0.0
Internal relays (M)Software relays/flags with no terminal: latches, intermediate logic.M0.0
Timer memory (T)Preset (PT), elapsed (ET) and status bits (timing, done).T1
Counter memory (C)Preset (PV), current value (CV), done bit.C1
Data registers (word)16/32-bit numbers: set-points, ADC readings, arithmetic results.MW10

1.5 Input and Output Devices and Modules

  • Discrete (digital) devices give on/off signals: push buttons, selector switches, limit switches, proximity sensors (inductive, capacitive), photoelectric sensors, float and pressure switches.
  • Analog devices give a signal proportional to the variable: thermocouples, RTDs, pressure and level transmitters (4–20 mA or 0–10 V).
  • Output types: relay outputs (a.c. or d.c., isolated, slow, limited life — the 1215C “Relay” version), transistor outputs (d.c. only, fast, long life), triac outputs (a.c. only).
  • Input modules isolate the CPU from the field by opto-isolators: an LED driven by the input current shines on a photo-transistor, so a voltage spike in the field wiring cannot reach the CPU.

1.6 Sinking and Sourcing

Definitions (lecture)
The terms sourcing and sinking describe the way d.c. devices are connected to a PLC, i.e. the direction of conventional current at the PLC terminal. In sourcing, the PLC module is the source of current: an input device receives current from the input module, or an output module supplies current to the load. In sinking, the PLC terminal receives current: current flows from the input device into the input module, or from the load into the output module, and on to 0 V.
Rule for matching sensors
PNP sensor → sinking input (PLC common at 0 V). NPN sensor → sourcing input (PLC common at +24 V). The sensor and the input must be “opposite”: one supplies the current, the other takes it. If both try to source (or both sink), no current flows and the input never turns on.

1.7 Solved Past Questions

2024 · Q5(a)Draw a block diagram of a PLC showing the main functional items and how buses link them. Explain the function of each block.12Topic: PLC internal architecture and buses

Block diagram. Draw Fig. 1.2 (architecture with the three buses). In the exam it is enough to show: battery, user-program RAM, CPU with clock, system ROM, data RAM and I/O unit on a common address bus, control bus and data bus; the program panel connected to the I/O unit; and the I/O system bus going to the input channels (buffer, opto-coupler) and output channels (latch, driver interface, drivers such as relays).

Function of each block.

  1. CPU (microprocessor): controls and processes all operations. Its ALU performs arithmetic (add, subtract) and logic (AND, OR, NOT, XOR); its registers hold the data being worked on; its control unit times the operations. It fetches each instruction of the user program, executes it on the image-table data, and writes the results.
  2. Clock: supplies the timing pulses (typically 1–8 MHz) that set the speed of operation and synchronise every element.
  3. System ROM: permanent storage of the operating system (executive program) and fixed data supplied by the manufacturer — scanning routine, I/O update, communication and self-diagnostics.
  4. User-program RAM: stores the user’s control program; it can be changed by the programmer. Backed by the battery (or replaced by EEPROM/flash) so the program is not lost when power is off.
  5. Data RAM: stores the input and output image tables, timer and counter preset/accumulated values, internal relays and data registers used while the program runs.
  6. Battery: keeps the RAM contents (program and retentive data) through a power failure.
  7. Input/output unit: the interface between the internal buses and the external world. Input channels use opto-couplers for isolation and buffers; output channels use latches to hold the output value between updates, a driver interface and drivers (relays, transistors, triacs) to switch the loads.
  8. Program panel / programming device: PC or handheld unit used to enter, edit, download and monitor the program through the I/O unit.

How the buses link the blocks.

  • Data bus (two-way): carries the data words between the CPU, memories and I/O unit — e.g. the status of 16 inputs read in one operation.
  • Address bus (from the CPU): carries the address of the location being accessed, selecting which memory word or I/O port takes part in the transfer. nnn lines address 2n2^n2n locations.
  • Control bus: carries read/write, clock and interrupt signals that tell the selected device what to do and when.
  • System (I/O) bus: carries data between the I/O unit and the input/output ports.

A complete answer also mentions the external power supply (230 V a.c. → 24 V/5 V d.c.) and the communications interface (Fig. 1.1).

2024 · Q5(b)What is sinking and sourcing? Explain with examples.08Topic: sinking and sourcing I/O

Definition. Sinking and sourcing describe how d.c. devices are connected to a PLC, i.e. the direction of conventional current at the PLC terminal (§1.6):

  • Sourcing — the PLC terminal supplies current. For an input: the input device receives current from the input module (the module common is connected to +24 V). For an output: current flows out of the output terminal into the load and on to 0 V (the output provides positive voltage).
  • Sinking — the PLC terminal receives current. For an input: current flows from the device into the input terminal and out of the common to 0 V (the common is at 0 V). For an output: current flows from the +24 V supply through the load into the output terminal, which switches it to 0 V.

Examples.

  1. Sinking input with a PNP proximity sensor (Fig. 1.3 right): the brown wire goes to +24 V, blue to 0 V; the black (output) wire goes to I0.0; the module common 1M is at 0 V. When the sensor sees a target its PNP transistor switches +24 V onto I0.0, current flows into the input → I0.0 = 1. (Siemens: “Sink wiring: PLC common gets 0 V; sink wiring uses PNP sensor.”)
  2. Sourcing input with an NPN sensor (Fig. 1.3 left): common 1M at +24 V; the NPN sensor connects I0.0 to 0 V when it switches, so current flows out of the input terminal into the sensor → I0.0 = 1. (“Source wiring: PLC common gets 24 V; uses NPN sensor.”)
  3. Sourcing (PNP transistor) output driving a solenoid valve: Q0.0 supplies +24 V to the coil, whose other end is at 0 V.
  4. Sinking (NPN transistor) output driving a lamp: the lamp is connected between +24 V and Q0.0; the output switches it to 0 V.
Exam tip
Draw one input pair (Fig. 1.3) and one output pair (Fig. 1.4) with the current arrows, and state the matching rule: PNP ↔ sinking input, NPN ↔ sourcing input. Relay outputs are neither: they are dry contacts that can be wired either way.

2. Ladder Diagrams, Logic Functions and Function Block Diagrams ★★★

2.1 The Ladder Diagram

Definition
A ladder diagram (LAD) is the graphical PLC programming language that looks like a relay wiring diagram. It consists of two vertical lines representing the power rails and horizontal lines between them, the rungs of the ladder. Each rung holds input conditions (contacts) on the left and an output (coil or function box) on the right. When there is a continuous path of “power flow” from the left rail through closed contacts to the output, the output is energised. It is one of the five IEC 61131-3 languages: ladder diagram (LD), instruction list (IL), sequential function chart (SFC), structured text (ST) and function block diagram (FBD).

A switch in series with a motor across L1 and L2 (a relay circuit) becomes, in ladder form, a contact and a coil between the two rails. The ladder is a picture of logic, not of wiring: the contact named I0.0 represents the state of input I0.0 in the input image table, and the coil Q0.0 writes a bit in the output image table.

Rules for drawing ladder diagrams (lecture and Bolton §5.1):

  1. The vertical lines are the power rails; power is considered to flow from the left rail to the right rail.
  2. Each rung defines one operation of the controlled process. A rung must start with inputs (contacts) and end with at least one output (coil or box).
  3. Electrical devices are shown in their normal (unenergised) condition: a normally open (NO) contact is drawn open, a normally closed (NC) contact closed. An NO contact passes power when its bit is 1 (“examine if closed”); an NC contact passes power when its bit is 0 (“examine if open”).
  4. A particular device can appear in more than one rung (any number of contacts may use the same address), but an output coil address should be used only once as a coil.
  5. Inputs and outputs are identified by their addresses (I0.0, Q0.0, M0.0 — Siemens; X400, Y430, M100 — Mitsubishi; I:012/01 — Allen-Bradley).
  6. Rungs are read and executed from left to right, and the program from top to bottom; the last rung is END.

2.2 The Scan Cycle

While a PLC is in RUN mode the CPU executes the main program cyclically. One scan consists of (lecture slide 9 and memory-organization flowchart):

  1. Input scan — the states of all physical inputs are read and copied into the input image table (process-image input). They are then held constant for the rest of the scan, even if a switch changes meanwhile.
  2. Program scan — the instructions are fetched, decoded and executed in order, rung 1 to END. In each rung the contacts are evaluated from left to right using the image-table values; the result (the “power flow”, or result of logic operation, RLO) is written to the coil bit in the output image table. A result written by one rung is immediately seen by every rung below it.
  3. Output scan — the output image table is copied to the physical output terminals (through the latches). Outputs keep these values until the next output scan.
  4. Housekeeping — communication with the programming device/HMI, self-diagnostics, watchdog reset; then the cycle repeats.

This method is called mass I/O copying; the alternative, continuous updating, reads each input as it is needed during the program and is slower for large I/O counts. The time for one complete cycle is the scan (cycle) time, typically about 1–50 ms. It depends on the CPU, the size of the program, the number of I/O points and the system functions in use.

Consequences of scanning
  • An input must last longer than one scan or it may be missed. With a 40 ms scan the maximum pulse rate that can be detected is 1/0.04=251/0.04 = 251/0.04=25 Hz; faster signals need high-speed counter inputs.
  • The response time to an input can be up to about two scans.
  • Rung order matters. A bit set late in the program is not seen by earlier rungs until the next scan — the basis of the one-shot circuit (§4.3).
  • If the same coil is written in two rungs, only the last rung counts (“double-coil” error).

2.3 Logic Functions in Ladder Form

AND is contacts in series; OR is contacts in parallel (branches); NOT is a normally closed contact. Combinations give NAND, NOR and XOR.

ABAND A⋅BA\cdot BA⋅BOR A+BA+BA+BNAND A⋅B‾\overline{A\cdot B}A⋅BNOR A+B‾\overline{A+B}A+B​XOR A⊕BA\oplus BA⊕B
0000110
0101101
1001101
1111000
Useful identities (De Morgan)
A⋅B‾=A‾+B‾(NAND = NC contacts in parallel),A+B‾=A‾⋅B‾(NOR = NC contacts in series)\overline{A\cdot B}=\overline{A}+\overline{B}\quad(\text{NAND = NC contacts in parallel}),\qquad \overline{A+B}=\overline{A}\cdot\overline{B}\quad(\text{NOR = NC contacts in series})A⋅B=A+B(NAND = NC contacts in parallel),A+B​=A⋅B(NOR = NC contacts in series) A⊕B=A⋅B‾+A‾⋅B(XOR = two branches, each one NO and one NC)A\oplus B=A\cdot\overline{B}+\overline{A}\cdot B\quad(\text{XOR = two branches, each one NO and one NC})A⊕B=A⋅B+A⋅B(XOR = two branches, each one NO and one NC)

2.4 Latching and Multiple Outputs

A latch (seal-in) keeps an output on after a momentary start input has been released: a contact of the output itself is placed in parallel with the start button, and an NC stop contact is placed in series. The rung is Q=(Start+Q)⋅Stop‾Q=(\text{Start}+Q)\cdot\overline{\text{Stop}}Q=(Start+Q)⋅Stop​. Lecture example (slide 20): a motor controlled by stop and start push buttons, with one signal lamp on when power is applied to the motor and another when it is not:

Rung 1 latches Q0.0 when Start is pressed and drops it when Stop is pressed. Rung 2 uses an NO contact of Q0.0 for the “running” lamp, rung 3 an NC contact of Q0.0 for the “stopped” lamp — one output can have as many contacts as needed. (In a real plant the stop button is wired NC and programmed NO; see §10.2.)

2.5 Function Block Diagrams and Boolean Algebra

A function block diagram (FBD) is a graphical language that shows signal and data flow through blocks — reusable software elements. Each block is a rectangle with the function name inside (AND “&”, OR “≥1”, NOT “1”, XOR “=1”, TON, CTU …), inputs on the left and outputs on the right. A small circle on an input or output means negation (NOT). Lines connect outputs to inputs; signals flow from left to right. FBD is natural for engineers used to logic gates and for continuous (analog/PID) control.

Converting between Boolean expressions, FBD and ladder. Each AND term becomes contacts in series; each OR becomes parallel branches; each complemented variable becomes an NC contact. Conversely, read the ladder rung as a Boolean expression and draw one gate per operator. Example (lecture, pump task): a pump is to run when the start switch is closed, the tank level is below the required level and there is liquid in the reservoir — Pump = Start · LowLevel · Reservoir: three NO contacts in series, or a three-input AND block.

2.6 Deriving a Ladder Program from a Timing Chart

Method
  1. Mark every instant at which any signal changes; this divides the chart into intervals.
  2. For each interval write the input combination and the output value (a truth table).
  3. If the same input combination always gives the same output, the logic is combinational: write the sum-of-products expression for the rows with output 1, simplify, and draw it.
  4. If the same input combination gives different outputs at different times, the output depends on history: use a latch (seal-in contact of the output, or SET/RESET coils), a timer or a counter.
  5. Check the ladder by replaying the chart interval by interval.

2.7 Solved Past Questions

2022 · Q5(a) | 2023 · Q5(a)What is Ladder diagram? How is the scanning operation occurred in a Ladder diagram?10Topic: ladder diagram and scan cycle

Ladder diagram. A ladder diagram is the most widely used PLC programming language. It is drawn like the rungs of a ladder between two vertical power rails. Each horizontal rung carries input conditions — normally open contacts —| |— and normally closed contacts —|/|— — on the left, and an output coil —( )— or a function box (timer, counter, move) on the right. If there is a continuous path of “power flow” through closed contacts from the left rail to the output, the output is energised (Fig. 2.1). Series contacts give AND, parallel contacts give OR, NC contacts give NOT. The program ends with an END rung. The ladder represents logic, not physical wiring: each contact reads a bit of the PLC memory, so one input can be used in many rungs.

Scanning operation. The PLC executes the ladder program repeatedly in a scan cycle (Fig. 2.3):

  1. Input scan: the CPU reads all physical inputs and stores their states in the input image table. These stored values are used for the whole scan.
  2. Program scan: the CPU starts at rung 1 and examines each rung from left to right, evaluating the contacts with the image-table values. If the rung is true it sets the output bit, otherwise it clears it, in the output image table. It then moves to the next rung, top to bottom, until the END rung. A result written by a rung is available to all following rungs in the same scan.
  3. Output scan: the output image table is transferred to the physical outputs, which hold their states until the next update.
  4. Housekeeping: communication and self-diagnostics; the watchdog checks that the scan finished in time. The cycle then repeats.

The time for one cycle is the scan time (typically 1–50 ms). Because of scanning, inputs must last longer than one scan time to be seen (e.g. 40 ms scan → at most 25 pulses per second), the order of rungs affects the result, and outputs change only once per scan.

3. Instruction Lists and Sequential Function Charts ★★★

3.1 Instruction List (IL)

Definition (lecture)
An instruction list (IL) is a text programming method that can be thought of as entering a ladder program as text. The program is a series of instructions, each on a new line. An instruction consists of an operator (a mnemonic code such as LD, AND, OR, OUT) followed by one or more operands (the subjects of the operator, e.g. X400 or I0.0). Each operator corresponds to a ladder element. Each instruction either uses or changes the value stored in a memory register — the result register (accumulator, RLO). The mnemonics differ between manufacturers, but IEC 1131-3 (now IEC 61131-3) defines a standard set.

Example (lecture slide 4):

OperatorOperandComment
LDA(* Load A into the result register *)
ANDB(* AND B with the register *)
STQ(* Store the result in Q, i.e. output to Q *)

Text between (* and *) is a comment and is not executed. A label followed by a colon can mark an entry point for jumps, e.g. PUMP_OK: LD C.

IEC 61131-3MitsubishiOMRONSiemensOperationLadder element
LDLDLDALoad operand into result registerStart a rung with an NO contact
LDNLDILD NOTANLoad negated operandStart a rung with an NC contact
ANDANDANDABoolean ANDSeries NO contact
ANDNANIAND NOTANAND with negated operandSeries NC contact

Table 3.1 Instruction-code mnemonics (lecture Table 6.1). In Siemens STL, A/AN also start a rung (first check).

3.2 Branches and Several Rungs

Simple logic. AND: LD X400 · AND X401 · OUT Y430 (Siemens A I0.1 · A I0.2 · = Q2.0). OR: LD X400 · OR X401 · OUT Y430 (A I0.1 · O I0.2 · = Q2.0). NOR: LDI X400 · ANI X401 · OUT Y430. NAND: LDI X400 · ORI X401 · OUT Y430.

Branch codes. When whole blocks of contacts are combined, the PLC must hold one block’s result while it evaluates the next:

  • Mitsubishi: each block starts with a new LD/LDI; ORB (OR block) puts the last two blocks in parallel, ANB (AND block) puts them in series.
  • Siemens: brackets — A( … ) and O( … ) — open and close a nested expression.
  • IEC 61131-3: deferred operators with brackets, e.g. AND( … ), OR( … ).
Two series pairs in parallel: (A⋅B‾)+(A‾⋅B)(A\cdot\overline{B})+(\overline{A}\cdot B)(A⋅B)+(A⋅B)Two parallel pairs in series: (A+C)⋅(B+D)(A+C)\cdot(B+D)(A+C)⋅(B+D)
Mitsubishi: LD X400 · ANI X401 · LDI X400 · AND X401 · ORB · OUT Y430
Siemens: A( · A I0.0 · AN I0.1 · ) · O( · AN I0.0 · A I0.1 · ) · = Q2.0		 Mitsubishi: LD X400 · OR X402 · LD X401 · OR X403 · ANB · OUT Y430
Siemens: A( · A I0.0 · O I0.2 · ) · A( · A I0.1 · O I0.3 · ) · = Q2.0

More than one rung. Each rung starts again with LD: a rung with input A driving output A, and a rung with input A NC driving output B, is LD X400 · OUT Y430 · LDI X400 · OUT Y431 (Siemens A I0.0 · = Q2.0 · AN I0.0 · = Q2.1). An internal relay is programmed like an output: LD X400 · OR X402 · AND X401 · OUT M100 · LD M100 · AND X403 · OUT Y430 (lecture: Internal Relay slide 8).

3.3 Structured Text (ST) in Brief

ST is a Pascal-like high-level IEC language: assignments Q := (A AND B) OR C;, IF … THEN … ELSE … END_IF, CASE, FOR and WHILE loops, and calls of timers and counters. It suits calculations and decision-heavy code; ladder suits interlocks and sequences that technicians must read.

3.4 Sequential Function Charts (SFC)

Definition (lecture)
A sequential function chart (SFC) is a pictorial representation of a system’s operation that shows the sequence of events involved in it. The operation is divided into steps (states) joined by transitions; each step has its actions. It is the IEC 61131-3 language (derived from GRAFCET) for sequential control.

Elements and rules (lecture):

  1. Steps: the operation is described by separate, sequentially connected states or steps, shown as rectangular boxes, each representing one particular state of the controlled system. The initial step — the state in which the system is held ready to start — is drawn as a double box.
  2. Transitions: each connecting line between steps carries a short horizontal bar with the transition condition that must be satisfied before the system can move from one step to the next. Two steps can never be directly connected; they must be separated by a transition. Two transitions can never follow each other directly; they must be separated by a step.
  3. When the transition condition is realised, the next step becomes active and the previous one inactive.
  4. The process continues from step to step until the complete machine cycle is finished (and usually loops back to the start).
  5. Actions: outputs/actions at a step are drawn as boxes linked horizontally to the step and occur while that step is active. The behaviour of an action can be written in ladder, FBD, IL or ST inside the box.
  6. Qualifiers in front of an action specify how it behaves: N (or none) — non-stored, executed continually while the step is active; P — pulse, executed once when the step is activated; D — time-delayed, starts after a specified time; L — time-limited, ends after a specified time (e.g. “L T#5s”); S/R — stored (set) and reset.
  7. Directed links connect steps and transitions; the normal flow is from top to bottom, and an arrow is used for any link that goes upwards (loop).
  • Selective branching: the step that follows State 0 depends on which transition (IN1, IN2 or IN3) occurs; only one path is taken. Drawn with a single horizontal line, a transition on each branch.
  • Parallel branching: when the single transition IN1 occurs, States 1, 2 and 3 all become active simultaneously. Drawn with a double horizontal line.
  • Convergence (selective): State 4 follows when either IN4 (from State 2) or IN5 (from State 3) occurs.
  • Simultaneous convergence: parallel paths join at a double line; when IN4 occurs State 4 follows from States 2 and 3 (in the lecture’s ladder, the State-2 and State-3 outputs are in parallel, followed by IN4).

SFC ↔ ladder. Each step is an output (or internal relay) of a rung whose conditions are “previous step active AND transition true”. Example: Step 0 is set when IN1 occurs (OUT 1); Step 1 is set when OUT 1 is on and IN2 occurs (OUT 2). Selective branching gives several rungs, each with the same previous-step contact and a different input. Parallel branching gives one rung driving several outputs. General convergence gives parallel branches (State 2 · IN4) + (State 3 · IN5); simultaneous convergence gives (State 2 + State 3) · IN4.

3.5 Solved Past Questions

Instruction list. An instruction list is a textual PLC language in which the program is entered as a list of instructions, one per line. Each instruction is an operator (mnemonic) followed by an operand (address), and it uses or changes the result register. Each operator corresponds to a ladder element: LD/LDI start a rung with an NO/NC contact, AND/ANI add series contacts, OR/ORI parallel contacts, ORB/ANB combine blocks, OUT drives the coil (Table 3.1). Comments in (* … *) explain the program.

[KEY IDENTITY]ORB (Mitsubishi) and O( … ) (Siemens) both mean “OR this whole series block with the previous one”.

Check: the result is Q=AB‾+A‾BQ=A\overline{B}+\overline{A}BQ=AB+AB — output on when exactly one input is on (truth table §2.3; simulated in calc.py: 0, 1, 1, 0).

Source lecturePriyo Sir · IL, SFC and ST programming methods (Instruction lists.pptx, slides 2–8)
2023 · Q6(c)Discuss data compression for PLC. Write down the instruction lists for the following Ladder programs shown below.10Topic: data compression · instruction lists
Note on the wording
“Data compression” is not a topic of the lecture slides; the slides teach data comparison (Data Handling deck). The answer below discusses data compression as asked and also summarises data comparison in case that was intended (full treatment in §9.3).

Data compression for PLC. Compression means storing or sending the same information with fewer bits or fewer records. In PLC systems it is used in three ways:

  1. Bit packing: many single-bit states (limit switches, alarms, step flags) are packed into one word. Sixteen status bits M10.0–M11.7 occupy one word MW10, which can be moved, compared or sent over a network with one MOVE instead of sixteen bit transfers. Shift registers and drum sequencers work on such packed words.
  2. Number coding: values are held in compact codes — BCD packs one decimal digit into 4 bits for thumbwheel inputs and displays; integers (16 bit) are used instead of REAL (32 bit) where the resolution is enough; scaled integers (e.g. level in mm) replace floating-point values.
  3. Data logging / communication compression: when a PLC or SCADA historian records process values, it stores a new value only when it changes by more than a deadband (report-by-exception), or uses swinging-door/run-length methods. This greatly reduces memory use and network traffic, at the cost of a small, known error.

Data comparison (if intended): comparison instructions (=, <>, >, >=, <, <=) compare two data values, e.g. an analog reading with a set-point, and give a 1/0 result that acts like a contact (§9.3).

Step 1 — left program (XOR: [X400 · NOT X401] OR [NOT X400 · X401] → Q1), Mitsubishi style:

StepInstruction
0LD X400
1ANI X401
2LDI X400
3AND X401
4ORB
5OUT Q1

In IEC/Siemens bracket form: A( · A X400 · AN X401 · ) · O( · AN X400 · A X401 · ) · = Q1.

Step 2 — right program (NOT X400 · X401 → Q1):

StepInstruction
0LDI X400
1AND X401
2OUT Q1

IEC: LDN X400 · AND X401 · ST Q1; Siemens: AN X400 · A X401 · = Q1.

[DATA EXTRACTED]The paper mixes Mitsubishi inputs (X400, X401) with an output called Q1; the operand names are kept exactly as printed.

Check: left: Q1 = 0, 1, 1, 0 for (X400, X401) = 00, 01, 10, 11; right: Q1 = 1 only for X400 = 0, X401 = 1 (simulated, calc.py).

2022 · Q6(b)What is sequential function chart? Draw the sequential function chart for the following ladder diagram shown in Figure 6(b).12Topic: SFC from a ladder program

Sequential function chart: a graphical IEC 61131-3 language that describes a sequential process as steps (rectangles; initial step double-framed) connected through transitions (short bars with a condition) and with actions attached to the steps; steps and transitions must alternate; branches may be selective (single line) or parallel (double line) (§3.4).

Step 1 — rung 1 (IN 0 → OUT 0): from the start, transition IN 0 activates State 0, action OUT 0.

Step 2 — rung 2 (OUT 0 · IN 1 → OUT 1 and OUT 2): one transition (IN 1) after State 0 activates two states at the same time — a parallel branch (double line) to State 1 (OUT 1) and State 2 (OUT 2).

Step 3 — rungs 3 and 4: in the left path, OUT 1 · IN 3 → State 3 (OUT 3); in the right path, OUT 2 · IN 4 → State 4 (OUT 4).

Step 4 — rung 5 ((OUT 3 + OUT 4) · IN5 → OUT 5): the two paths join and a single transition IN 5 leads to State 5. In the lecture this ladder pattern (state outputs in parallel, then one input) is the simultaneous convergence (double line).

Step 5 — rung 6: END closes the program.

[KEY IDENTITY]One rung with several output coils = parallel branch; parallel state contacts followed by one input = simultaneous convergence.
Remark
The ladder of Figure 6(b) is a simplified textbook ladder (Bolton problem): the coils do not latch and nothing resets the earlier states, and strictly the ladder lets OUT 5 come on when either OUT 3 or OUT 4 is on (checked by simulation). The SFC above is the intended answer of the lecture (6. SFC, p. 8).
Source lecturePriyo Sir · 6 – Sequential function charts (6. SFC.pdf, pp. 1–8); IL, SFC and ST programming methods (Instruction lists.pptx, slides 13–16)
2023 · Q5(c)What is sequential function chart? Describe the elements of a sequential function chart.10Topic: SFC elements

A sequential function chart (SFC) is a pictorial (graphical) PLC programming language, standardised in IEC 61131-3 and derived from GRAFCET, used to represent the operation of a system as a sequence of events. The process is divided into steps; the program moves from one step to the next when the conditions between them are met; and at each step the required actions are performed (Fig. 3.1).

Elements:

  1. Initial step: a double-framed rectangle; the state in which the system waits ready to start. Exactly one initial step per chart.
  2. Steps (states): rectangles, numbered or named, each representing one state of the controlled system. A step is either active or inactive.
  3. Transitions: a short horizontal bar on the vertical link between two steps, with its transition condition (a Boolean expression of inputs, timers, counters). When the preceding step is active and the condition becomes true, the next step is activated and the preceding one deactivated.
  4. Directed links: vertical lines connecting steps and transitions; flow is top to bottom; an arrow marks an upward (loop-back) link.
  5. Actions: rectangles attached to the right of a step, describing the outputs or operations performed while the step is active; their behaviour may be written in LD, FBD, IL or ST.
  6. Action qualifiers: N (non-stored, while active), S (stored/set), R (reset), P (pulse, once on entry), D (delayed), L (time-limited).
  7. Branches: selective (single horizontal line, one path chosen by the first true transition) and parallel (double horizontal line, all paths start together).
  8. Convergence: selective convergence (single line, any path) and simultaneous convergence (double line, all parallel paths must be complete).

Rules: steps and transitions must alternate — two steps are never directly linked and two transitions are never directly linked; the chart forms a closed loop for a repeating machine cycle.

Source lecturePriyo Sir · 6 – Sequential function charts (6. SFC.pdf, pp. 1–9); IL, SFC and ST programming methods (Instruction lists.pptx, slides 11–15)

4. Internal Relays: Latching, Battery-Backed, One-Shot, Set/Reset and MCR ★★★

4.1 Internal Relays

Definition (lecture)
An internal relay is a PLC element that holds data in the form of a bit and is used like a relay to switch other parts of the program on or off. It does not exist as a real-world switching device: it is an imaginary, programmed relay — merely a bit in the storage memory — that has a coil and any number of contacts but is not connected to any physical output. It is also called an auxiliary relay, marker, flag, bit storage or coil.
  • Its coil is drawn with the output symbol —( )— and an internal-relay address; its contacts are drawn with the input symbols —| |— or —|/|— and carry the same address.
  • Addressing: Mitsubishi M100, M101 (auxiliary relay/marker); Siemens F0.0 (flag; M0.0 or %M0.0 in S7-1200, where the 1215C has 8 KB of markers %M0.0 … %M8191.7); Telemecanique B0, B1 (bit); Toshiba R000 (internal relay); Allen-Bradley B3/001 (bit storage).
  • Even a small PLC has a hundred or more; some are battery-backed (retentive).

Uses. (1) Programs with multiple input conditions: a group of conditions energises a marker, and the marker’s contacts are combined with other inputs in later rungs; (2) latching — holding a state after a momentary input; (3) storing intermediate results and flags (step flags, “cycle done”, “fault”); (4) one-shot pulses; (5) master control of groups of rungs; (6) building shift registers (Ch. 8).

Lecture example — rubbing machine. A machine must move down each time it is up and up each time it is down (reciprocating motion), starting when Start is pressed and ending when Stop is pressed. Two latching rungs (down: I0.3 up-limit → Q0.2; up: I0.4 down-limit → Q0.3, each broken by the other limit) give the reciprocation but cannot be started or stopped. An internal relay M0.0 latched by Start (I1.0) and broken by Stop (I1.1) is placed in series in both rungs, so the motion runs only while M0.0 is on.

4.2 Battery-Backed (Retentive) Relays

If the supply is cut off while a PLC is running, all output relays and ordinary internal relays are turned off. When power returns, the contacts are in a different state from before the failure, so a machine that was in the middle of a sequence would restart at the wrong point — or not at all.

Battery-backed relay (lecture)
To overcome this, some internal relays have a battery backup so that they retain their state of activation even when the power supply is off. They are used in circuits that ensure a safe shutdown of a plant in the event of a power failure and enable it to restart in an appropriate manner. They are programmed with a retentive memory coil —(M)—.

Why a battery? The internal relays are bits in RAM, and RAM is volatile: its contents are lost when power is removed. A small lithium battery (or a large capacitor) keeps the RAM area of the retentive relays powered while the main supply is off. Mitsubishi reserves M300–M377 (FX) as battery-backed; on the S7-1200 no battery is needed because retentive data are copied to non-volatile memory at power-down — the retentive marker bytes are chosen in the CPU properties or with the “Retain” column of the tag table.

4.3 One-Shot Operation

A one-shot makes an internal relay’s contacts active for just one cycle (one scan), giving a fixed-duration pulse whatever the length of the input. It is used to count, to toggle, or to trigger an action once per button press.

Operation. When the trigger input occurs, rung 1 is true (the cycle-control contact is still closed) → trigger output on. Rung 2 then energises the cycle-control relay. Because rung 2 is executed after rung 1, its effect is not felt until the next scan, when the cycle-control NC contact opens rung 1 and the trigger output goes off. The output can occur again only after the trigger input has gone off and on again. Modern PLCs provide an edge contact —|P|— (Siemens, with an edge-memory bit) that does the same in one rung; an —|N|— contact pulses on the falling edge.

4.4 Set and Reset

The SET coil —(S)— switches its bit on when power reaches it, and the bit remains set (even after the rung goes false) until it is reset. The RESET coil —(R)— switches the bit off when power reaches it, and it remains off until it is set. Together they form a latch (flip-flop) without a seal-in contact; they are often in different rungs, even in different parts of the program.

Priority. If both set and reset are true together, the result depends on the priority (lecture slides 16–17):

  • SET priority (set-dominant) — the RS block (inputs R and S1; “1” marks the dominant input): set wins, Q = 1.
  • RESET priority (reset-dominant) — the SR block (inputs S and R1): reset wins, Q = 0.

With separate coils, the rung written last wins, because it is executed last in the scan.

4.5 Master Control Relay (MCR)

When a large number of outputs must be turned on or off together, a master control relay switches whole sections of the ladder program with one instruction. It acts like a relay in the left power rail of a zone: when it is energised, the rungs inside the zone are executed normally; when it is off, the outputs in the zone are switched off (non-retentive outputs de-energised) whatever their own inputs.

Siemens S7-300/400 used MCRA/MCR</MCR> instructions; the S7-1200 has no MCR coil, so a zone is built by ANDing an enable marker into each rung, by a JMP/label that skips the block, or by calling a function block conditionally. Each MC must be closed by an MCR (or MCR … END); a jump into an MC zone is not allowed.

4.6 Solved Past Questions

2022 · Q7(a)Define internal relay. What is the function of battery-backed relay in PLC?08Topic: internal and battery-backed relays

Internal relay. An internal relay is a bit in the PLC memory that behaves like a relay: it has a coil, which is energised by a rung like an output, and any number of NO/NC contacts, which are used in other rungs like inputs. It is not a physical relay and has no output terminal — it is an imaginary, programmed relay. It is also called an auxiliary relay, marker, flag or bit storage (Mitsubishi M100, Siemens F0.0/M0.0, Telemecanique B0, Toshiba R000). Internal relays are used to combine multiple input conditions, to latch states, to store flags and intermediate results, and to link one part of a program to another (Fig. 4.1).

Function of a battery-backed relay. On a power failure all outputs and ordinary internal relays go off, so after power returns a sequence would restart from the wrong point. A battery-backed internal relay retains its state while the power is off, because its memory is kept alive by a battery. It is therefore used to:

  • remember the state of the process (which step, which latches were on) through a power failure;
  • ensure a safe shutdown of the plant and let it restart in an appropriate manner, at the correct point;
  • keep latched outputs on after the power is restored (Fig. 4.2: IR1 stays energised and Out1 comes back on).

It is programmed with the retentive memory coil —(M)—.

Source lecturePriyo Sir · Ch 7 – Internal Relays (Internal Relay.pptx, slides 3–11)
2024 · Q8(b)What is a battery-backed relay? Why is a battery required in a battery-backed relay?05Topic: battery-backed relay

Battery-backed relay: an internal relay (marker) whose state is held by battery-supported memory, so that it retains its state of activation even when the PLC power supply is off. It is drawn as a retentive coil —(M)— and used to make a plant shut down safely on a power failure and restart at the correct point (Fig. 4.2).

Why a battery is required: internal relays are only bits in RAM. RAM is volatile — when the PLC supply fails, its contents are lost and every ordinary relay resets to 0. The battery keeps that part of the RAM powered during the outage, so the relay’s 1/0 state (and hence the latched outputs and the position in the sequence) survives. Without it the machine might restart at a different point in its sequence, which can be unsafe. (Newer PLCs such as the S7-1200 achieve the same by saving retentive data to flash at power-down.)

Source lecturePriyo Sir · Ch 7 – Internal Relays (Internal Relay.pptx, slides 9–11); Ch 7 – Internal Relays (S7-1215C) (Ch7_Internal_Relays_S7-1215C.pptx, slide 11)
2023 · Q6(a)Write short notes on master control relay and battery-backed relays with necessary ladder diagram.10Topic: MCR and battery-backed relays

Master control relay (MCR). When many outputs depend on one common condition, a master control relay turns whole sections of the ladder on or off with one instruction, like a relay switching the power rail of a zone. In Mitsubishi format (Fig. 4.8 left): input X400 energises MC N0 M100; rungs 2 and 3 (X401 → Y430, X402 → Y431) are between MC and MCR N0. While X400 is on, these rungs work normally; when X400 is off, Y430 and Y431 are off regardless of X401, X402. IL: LD X400, MC N0 M100, LD X401, OUT Y430, LD X402, OUT Y431, MCR N0. On S7-1200 the same effect is obtained with a zone marker in series with each rung (Fig. 4.8 right) or with a jump. Uses: an “enable/automatic mode” zone, a machine section that must be dead when a guard is open, test modes. Every MC must be closed by its MCR.

Battery-backed relays. Ordinary internal relays and outputs all go off when the power fails, so on restart a sequence would resume from the wrong point. Battery-backed relays keep their state through the power failure because their memory is supported by a battery; they use the retentive coil —(M)—. In Fig. 4.2, input In1 energises the battery-backed IR1 (M10.0), which latches itself; Out1 follows IR1. After a power failure IR1 is still set, so Out1 comes back on when power returns and the plant continues — or shuts down safely — from the correct point. A reset input releases the latch deliberately.

Source lecturePriyo Sir · Ch 7 – Internal Relays (Internal Relay.pptx, slides 9–11, 18–20); Ch 7 – Internal Relays (S7-1215C) (Ch7_Internal_Relays_S7-1215C.pptx, slides 10–11)
2024 · Q6(c)Devise ladder programs which can be used to: (i) Maintain an output on, even when the input ceases and when there is a power failure. (ii) Switch on an output for a time of one cycle following a brief input. (iii) Switch on the power to a set of rungs.15Topic: battery-backed latch · one-shot · MCR
Given Data (I/O allocation chosen)
(i) Input I0.0, reset I0.1, retentive marker M10.0, output Q0.0. (ii) Trigger input I0.0, cycle-control marker M0.1, output Q0.0. (iii) Zone-enable input I0.0 (X400), zone rungs I0.1 → Q0.0, I0.2 → Q0.1.

(i) Output maintained after the input ceases and through a power failure → battery-backed latch. Two requirements: a latch (output stays on when the input ceases) and retention (state survives a power failure). So the latch is built on a battery-backed (retentive) internal relay, which then drives the output — Fig. 4.2.

Rung 1: (I0.0 OR M10.0) AND NOT I0.1 → retentive coil M10.0. The input sets M10.0, and the M10.0 contact holds it after the input ceases.

Rung 2: M10.0 → Q0.0.

Check: input on → M10.0 = 1, Q0.0 = 1; input off → still 1; power fails → ordinary bits clear but M10.0 is retained → on restart rung 2 switches Q0.0 back on (simulated: retentive bit keeps Out1; an ordinary marker would lose it).

[KEY IDENTITY]Latch = output contact in parallel with the input; retention = the latching bit must be battery-backed.

(ii) Output for one cycle after a brief input → one-shot (Fig. 4.3).

Rung 1: I0.0 AND NOT M0.1 → Q0.0 (trigger output).

Rung 2: I0.0 → M0.1 (cycle control).

Check (scan by scan): scan 1 with I0.0 = 1: rung 1 true (M0.1 still 0) → Q0.0 = 1; rung 2 sets M0.1. Scan 2: M0.1 = 1 opens rung 1 → Q0.0 = 0, and it stays 0 until I0.0 goes off and on again. Q0.0 is on for exactly one scan (simulated: 0, 1, 0, 0 …).

[INTUITION]The trick is rung order: M0.1 is written after rung 1 has already used it.

Alternative: one rung with a positive-edge contact —|P|— on I0.0 driving Q0.0 (Fig. 4.4).

(iii) Switch on the power to a set of rungs → master control relay (Fig. 4.8): rung 1, X400 (I0.0) → MC N0 M100; zone rungs X401 → Y430 and X402 → Y431; final rung MCR N0. When the MC input is on, “power” reaches the left rail of the zone and the rungs work; when it is off, the outputs in the zone are de-energised. On S7-1200: rung 1 I0.0 → M1.0; every zone rung starts with an M1.0 contact.

2024 · Q7(b)Explain with examples how a SET/RESET (SR/RS) latch works.10Topic: SET/RESET latches

Principle. A SET/RESET latch is a memory element (flip-flop). A pulse on the set input makes its output Q = 1, and Q stays 1 after the set input disappears. A pulse on the reset input makes Q = 0, and Q stays 0. If neither input is active the output keeps its last state (memory). Ladder form: separate —(S)— and —(R)— coils with the same address (Fig. 4.5); block form: SR or RS boxes (Fig. 4.6).

Example 1 — motor start/stop with coils. Rung 1: Start I0.0 → SET Q0.0; rung 2: Stop I0.1 → RESET Q0.0. Pressing Start for an instant starts the motor; it keeps running after Start is released; pressing Stop stops it (Fig. 4.5 timing). No seal-in contact is needed.

The two priorities decide what happens when set and reset are both 1:

BlockBehaviourTypical use
SR (reset-dominant)Inputs S and R1. S alone → Q = 1; R1 alone → Q = 0; both → Q = 0 (reset wins).Safety: a stop/fault must always win over start.
RS (set-dominant)Inputs R and S1. Both → Q = 1 (set wins).An alarm that must remain on while the fault is present even if acknowledged.

Example 2 — timing chart (Fig. 4.7): Set pulses at 1–3 s and 6–9 s, Reset pulses at 4–5 s and 7–8 s. Both latches go on at 1 s and off at 4 s. During 7–8 s both inputs are 1: the SR output is 0, the RS output stays 1; at 8 s reset is released and the SR output returns to 1 because set is still on.

Truth table (Qn = previous state):

SetResetSR (reset-dominant)RS (set-dominant)
00Qn (hold)Qn (hold)
1011
0100
1101

With separate S and R coils, the coil in the lower rung wins because it is executed last (verified by simulation: Reset rung last → Q = 0; Set rung last → Q = 1).

5. Jump and Call (Subroutines) ★★★

5.1 The Jump Instruction

Definition (lecture)
A jump instruction enables part of a ladder program to be jumped over when certain conditions are met. It lets a program be designed so that if certain conditions are met certain events occur, and if they are not met other events occur — like an if–else in C.

When there is an input to In 1, its contact closes and the jump coil is energised, so the program jumps to the rung where the jump ends (the label) and continues from there, missing the intermediate rungs. When there is no input, the jump is not active and the program proceeds rung by rung. Outputs in skipped rungs are not updated: they keep the state they had when the jump began — an important design point (a valve left open stays open). Whether timers inside a skipped section keep timing depends on the PLC (many hold their value), so timers in jumped sections should be avoided or their effect checked.

  • Mitsubishi: CJP (conditional jump) to EJP (end of jump) with the same number, e.g. CJP 700 … EJP 700.
  • Allen-Bradley PLC-5: JMP with a number 000–255 jumps to the LBL instruction with the same number.
  • Siemens: JMP executes the jump if its input (RLO) is 1, JMPN if it is 0; the destination is a label (DEST) at the start of a network.

Jump within jump is possible (a jump inside a section that is itself jumped over). Jumps are used to skip a sequence that is not needed (e.g. manual vs automatic mode, a pedestrian phase, §6.6), to bypass logic when a sensor says so (§9.6) and to go to a fault routine (§10.5).

5.2 Subroutines (Call)

Definition (lecture)
Subroutines are small programs that perform specific tasks and can be called for use in larger programs by a call instruction. The advantage is that they can be called repeatedly to perform their task without having to be written out in full each time in the main program — like a function in C/C++. When the subroutine is finished, a return instruction sends control back to the main program at the instruction after the call.
  • Mitsubishi: when input 1 occurs, CALL P calls subroutine P; the subroutine is written after FEND (end of the main program), starts with the pointer P and ends with SRET, which returns to the main program.
  • Allen-Bradley: JSR (jump to subroutine) calls it; the subroutine begins with SBR and ends with RET.
  • Siemens: CALL a block (FC/FB) and RET to return, or — more commonly — a function box with EN (enable) and ENO (enable out). If EN is connected directly to the left rail, the block is called unconditionally every scan; if a logic condition precedes EN, the block is called only when the condition is true. Blocks can be chained by connecting the ENO of one to the EN of the next. This is especially useful with a library of standard subroutine blocks.

Advantages of subroutines: shorter main program; repeated tasks written once; easier testing and fault-finding (each block tested separately); standard library blocks re-used between projects; the scan time is reduced because a subroutine is executed only when it is called.

5.3 Solved Past Questions

2022 · Q7(b)What is meant by subroutine in ladder diagram for PLC programing? Explain with example.08Topic: subroutines (call and return)

Subroutine. A subroutine is a separate, small ladder program that performs a specific task and is executed only when the main program calls it with a call instruction. After its last rung, a return instruction transfers control back to the main program, which continues from the rung after the call. It is like a function in C: written once, called as often as required, avoiding repeated rungs (Fig. 5.3).

Example — box filling station. A conveyor brings boxes to a filling station. The main program runs the conveyor; when a box is at the station it calls the filling subroutine FC1 “Fill_Box”.

  1. Rung 1 of the main program latches the Run marker M0.0 (Start I0.0, Stop I0.1).
  2. Rung 2: when Run and “box at station” (I0.2) are both true, CALL FC1 is executed; otherwise FC1 is skipped, saving scan time.
  3. In FC1: the feed valve Q0.1 opens if the box is empty (I0.3); a 5 s timer T1 runs while the valve is open; when it times out the “box full” lamp Q0.2 lights; RET returns to the main program.
  4. Rung 3 of the main program runs the conveyor Q0.0.

In Mitsubishi form the call is LD X402 · CALL P1, the main program ends with FEND, and the subroutine is P1: … SRET; in Allen-Bradley form JSR … SBR … RET.

Source lecturePriyo Sir · Jump & Call (lab manual Exp. 6) (JUMP & CALL.pdf, pp. 3–4)
2023 · Q5(d)What is subroutines in Ladder diagram for PLC programming? Explain with example.07Topic: subroutines

Subroutines are small programs for specific tasks that are stored separately from the main ladder program and are run only when called by a CALL instruction; a return instruction (RET/SRET) at the end sends the program back to the rung after the call. They let a frequently used routine be written once and used many times, keep the main program short, and reduce scan time because they run only when needed.

Example (Mitsubishi format, lecture Fig. 4(a)): in the main program, LD X400 · CALL P — when input 1 (X400) occurs, subroutine P is called. The main program ends with FEND. After FEND the subroutine starts at pointer P, contains its own rungs (e.g. X401 → Y430, X402 → Y431) and ends with SRET, which returns to the instruction after CALL P. In Allen-Bradley: JSR calls, SBR marks the start and RET the end. In Siemens TIA Portal the subroutine is a function block placed as a box; a contact before its EN input makes the call conditional (Figs. 5.4 and 5.5 give a complete Siemens example: OB1 calls FC1 “Fill_Box” only when a box is at the station).

Source lecturePriyo Sir · Jump & Call (lab manual Exp. 6) (JUMP & CALL.pdf, pp. 3–4)

6. Timers ★★★

6.1 Types of Timer

A PLC timer is a software function that counts time-base pulses (1 ms, 10 ms, 100 ms, 1 s …) from an internal clock and changes the state of its output (done bit, Q) when the counted time reaches the preset value (PT). The elapsed time is held in the timer’s accumulator (ET). Some manufacturers treat a timer as a relay coil that is energised and whose contacts close after the delay (Mitsubishi T450 K50 = 5 s with a 0.1 s base); others (IEC, Siemens) treat it as a delay box with an input IN, preset PT, output Q and elapsed time ET.

TimerBehaviourTypical use
TON on-delayWhen IN goes 1, ET starts counting; Q goes 1 when ET = PT and stays 1 while IN = 1. When IN goes 0, Q and ET reset at once. If IN is shorter than PT, Q never comes on.Start a second motor 10 s after the first; ignore short sensor pulses.
TOF off-delayQ goes 1 at once when IN goes 1. When IN goes 0, ET starts; Q goes 0 when ET = PT. If IN returns before PT, the timing is cancelled and Q stays 1.Run a cooling fan for 3 min after a machine stops; stair lights.
TP pulseA rising edge at IN gives Q = 1 for exactly PT, whatever the length of IN; not retriggerable while running.Fixed-length pulse to a solenoid.
TONR retentive on-delayLike TON but ET is not reset when IN goes 0: it accumulates over several on-periods until PT is reached; a separate reset input R clears it.Total running hours of a pump; maintenance alarms.
Timer range (lecture)
A 16-bit timer counts up to 32 767 time-base units. Time base 1 s: 32 767 s=546.132\,767\ \text{s}=546.132767 s=546.1 min ≈9.1\approx 9.1≈9.1 h. Time base 0.1 s: 3 276.73\,276.73276.7 s =54.6=54.6=54.6 min. Longer times: cascade timers (§6.3) or combine a timer with a counter (§7.3).

6.2 Programming Timers

Sequencing (lecture exercise: outputs Q0.0, Q0.1, Q0.2 in sequence with 3 s delays): Q0.0 is latched by the start button; Q0.0 starts TON T1 (3 s); T1 switches on Q0.1 and starts T2 (3 s); T2 switches on Q0.2. A stop contact in the latch rung resets everything. Bolton’s motor-sequence example works the same way with an internal relay IR1 latched by Start, starting timers T1 and T2 together with different presets so that motor 2 and motor 3 start after their delays.

Start/stop with delays (lecture exercise): motor 1 (Q0.0) starts on the rising edge of I0.0 and motor 2 (Q0.1) 10 s later — TON driven by Q0.0; when I0.0 falls motor 1 stops and motor 2 stops 10 s later — TOF on the motor-2 rung.

6.3 Cascaded Timers and On–Off Cycle Timers

Timers can be linked so that the done contact of one starts the next — cascading. The total delay is the sum of the presets, so times longer than one timer’s maximum can be obtained. Example (Bolton Fig. 9.7): timer 1 = 999 s started by In 1; its contact starts timer 2 = 100 s; timer 2 switches on the output, so the output comes on 999+100=1099999+100=1099999+100=1099 s after In 1. In Mitsubishi IL: LD X400 · OUT T450 K999 · LD T450 · OUT T451 K100 · LD T451 · OUT Y430.

On–off cycle timer. Two on-delay timers in a loop produce a repeating output: T1 (5 s) is started by In 1 and by an NC contact of T2; T1 done switches the output on and starts T2 (5 s); T2 done opens T1’s rung, which resets T1 and hence T2, and the cycle repeats: output 5 s off, 5 s on.

6.4 Interlocks and Motor Reversing

A reversing motor has two contactors (forward and reverse) that must never be energised together — that would short two supply phases. The standard protection is an interlock: an NC contact of each contactor in the other’s rung (in the program, and also hard-wired with the contactors’ auxiliary contacts). A motor that is still turning should not be plugged into the opposite direction, so a run-down delay is added: the new direction is enabled only after both contactors have been off for the stopping time.

6.5 Traffic-Light Sequence

Each state is timed by an on-delay timer; the done bit of one timer starts the next (cascade), and the last timer resets the chain so the cycle repeats. The lamps are decoded from the timer bits.

Cascaded timers are timers linked so that the output (done contact) of one timer is the input of the next. The second timer starts only when the first has timed out, so the delays add: ttotal=PT1+PT2+…t_{\text{total}}=PT_1+PT_2+\dotsttotal​=PT1​+PT2​+…. It is used (1) to obtain delays longer than the maximum preset of one timer (e.g. 32 767 × time base), and (2) to produce a sequence of events at successive times.

Rung 1: input I0.0 (X400) starts timer 1 with preset 999 s.

Rung 2: after 999 s, T1’s contact closes and starts timer 2 with preset 100 s.

Rung 3: after a further 100 s, T2’s contact closes and the output Q0.0 (Y430) is energised.

Given Data
S1 forward push button I0.0; S2 reverse push button I0.1; Stop push button I0.2 (assumed, needed to stop the motor); coil-1 = forward contactor Q0.0; coil-2 = reverse contactor Q0.1; run-down (stopping) time ≈ 10 s → TON T1, PT = 10 s; request markers M0.0 (forward), M0.1 (reverse).

Step 1 — requests (rungs 1, 2). Pressing S1 latches the forward request M0.0; pressing S2 latches M0.1. Each request rung contains an NC contact of the other button, so pressing S1 cancels the reverse request and vice versa — this is “S1 pressed → coil-2 de-energised”. Stop clears both.

Step 2 — rest timer (rung 3). T1 times while both coils are off. After 10 s the motor is assumed to be at rest and T1 = 1.

Step 3 — contactors (rungs 4, 5). Coil-1 = M0.0 · (T1 + Q0.0) · NOT Q0.1. It can start only when the motor is at rest (T1) and then holds itself (seal-in Q0.0), because T1 resets as soon as a coil is on. The NC Q0.1 contact is the interlock. Coil-2 is the mirror image.

[KEY IDENTITY]Interlock: each contactor’s NC contact in the other’s rung — the two directions can never be on together.

Sequence trace (simulated, Fig. 6.7): at power-up both coils are off and T1 times out after 10 s. 12 s: S1 pressed → coil-1 on at once (motor was at rest). 30 s: S2 pressed → reverse request set, forward request and coil-1 drop at once (“coil-1 de-energised”), T1 starts; 40 s: T1 done → coil-2 on. 60 s: S1 pressed → coil-2 de-energised immediately, coil-1 energised 10 s later at 70 s. 80 s: Stop → both off. At no instant are both coils on.

Reversal is delayed 10 s; coil-1 and coil-2 interlocked; S1 drops coil-2 at once.

(iii) Add a counter to count how many times the pedestrian crossing was used.15Topic: timers, jump and counter in one design
Interpretation (stated assumptions)
“3-way” is taken as a junction with three approaches A, B and C, served one at a time. Each direction’s own segment of the cycle is green 10 s → yellow 3 s → red 10 s; the 10 s red is an all-red clearance step timed by that direction’s own TON before the next direction gets green, and the direction then stays red while the others are served. A pedestrian request (push button) is stored and served at the end of the current cycle by a 10 s all-red WALK phase. JUMP instructions skip the sequence that is not in use: the vehicle sequence is jumped over during the walk phase, and the pedestrian sequence is jumped over when there is no request.
Given Data (I/O allocation)
Inputs: Start I0.0, Stop I0.1, pedestrian button I0.2. Outputs: A red/yellow/green Q0.0/Q0.1/Q0.2; B Q0.3/Q0.4/Q0.5; C Q0.6/Q0.7/Q1.0; WALK lamp Q1.1. Markers: Run M0.0, pedestrian request M1.0, pedestrian phase M1.1. Timers T1–T9 (A G 10, Y 3, R 10; B G 10, Y 3, R 10; C G 10, Y 3, R 10), T10 walk 10 s. Counter C1, display word MW10.

Step 1 — vehicle sequence (rungs 5–13). Nine TON timers in a cascade: T1 is started by Run · NOT T9, each next timer by the previous done bit. Cycle 3×(10+3+10)=693\times(10+3+10)=693×(10+3+10)=69 s; T9 done resets the whole chain.

Step 2 — lamp decoding (rungs 14–22). A green = Run · T1‾\overline{T1}T1; A yellow = T1⋅T2‾T1\cdot\overline{T2}T1⋅T2; A red = T2T2T2. B green = T3⋅T4‾T3\cdot\overline{T4}T3⋅T4; B yellow = T4⋅T5‾T4\cdot\overline{T5}T4⋅T5; B red = Run · (T3‾+T5\overline{T3}+T5T3+T5). C green = T6⋅T7‾T6\cdot\overline{T7}T6⋅T7; C yellow = T7⋅T8‾T7\cdot\overline{T8}T7⋅T8; C red = Run · (T6‾+T8\overline{T6}+T8T6+T8).

Step 3 — pedestrian request (rungs 2–3). The button SETs M1.0. At the end of a cycle (T9 done, all approaches red) a stored request SETs the pedestrian-phase marker M1.1.

Step 4 — jumps (rungs 4, 23, 24, 28). Rung 4: M1.1 → JMP VEH skips the vehicle sequence and lamp rungs (they hold “all red”). Rung 24: NOT M1.1 → JMP PED skips the pedestrian sequence in normal running.

Step 5 — pedestrian sequence (rungs 25–27). M1.1 starts T10 (10 s) and CTU C1 counts one use per phase (rising edge of M1.1); WALK = M1.1 · NOT T10; T10 done resets M1.0 and M1.1, so the vehicle sequence resumes with A green.

Step 6 — display (rung 29). MOVE C1.CV → MW10 shows the number of crossings.

[KEY IDENTITY]Rungs skipped by a jump are not executed: their outputs hold their last state (all red). The vehicle timers are all done at that moment, so the design works whether or not the PLC keeps updating them.

Checks (simulation, calc.py): no two greens are ever on together; WALK never overlaps a green; one button press gives exactly one 10 s walk and C1 = 1.

Cycle 69 s (+10 s WALK when requested); C1 counts crossings → MW10

7. Counters and Sequencers ★★★

7.1 Counters

Definition (lecture)
A counter is set to some preset number value and, when this number of input pulses has been received, it operates its contacts: normally open contacts close and normally closed contacts open. Down-counters count down from the preset value to zero, i.e. events are subtracted from the set value; when the counter reaches zero its contacts change state (most PLCs offer down counting). Up-counters count from zero up to the preset value; when the count reaches the set value its contacts change state.

A counter can be considered to consist of two basic elements: one relay coil (or input) to count input pulses and one to reset the counter, its contacts being used in other rungs. Each count is triggered by the rising edge (0 → 1) of the count input, so a long input pulse counts only once. Counters are retentive: the count is kept until a reset.

Vendor forms (lecture slide 4): Mitsubishi — counter C460 K10 with a separate RST C460 rung and an OUT C460 rung; Siemens — S_CU box (CU count input, S set, PV preset, R reset; outputs Q, CV in binary and CV_BCD), or the IEC CTU/CTD/CTUD boxes in TIA Portal; Toshiba — counter box with C (count) and E (enable/reset) inputs; Allen-Bradley — CTU C5:1 with Preset 10, done bit C5:1/DN used as a contact, RES C5:1 to reset (CTD counts down).

7.2 Up and Down Counting

To count items entering and leaving (a conveyor line, a car park), one counter counts up for items entering and down for items leaving. The output (e.g. “No empty spaces”) is triggered when the number entering exceeds the number leaving by the saturation value. In IEC form a single CTUD block has both CU and CD inputs; its QU output is 1 when CV ≥ PV.

7.3 Timers with Counters

A 16-bit timer can count only up to 32 767 time-base units (9.1 h with a 1 s base). Longer times are obtained by letting a timer generate periodic pulses and counting them. Example (lecture slide 7, Allen-Bradley): timer T4:0 with a 1 s base and preset 3600 resets itself every hour (its own DN contact in its rung); counter C5:0 with preset 24 counts the hourly pulses, so the output turns on after 24 h.

7.4 Sequencers and the Drum Sequencer

The drum sequencer is a form of counter used for sequential control. It replaces the mechanical drum sequencer, which controlled machines with a stepped, repeatable sequence of operations: a drum carried protruding pegs; as the drum rotated, contacts aligned with the pegs were closed when a peg struck them and opened when the peg had passed. Each row of pegs is one output; each angular position is one step.

The PLC sequencer consists of a master counter with a range of preset counts corresponding to the different steps. As it progresses through the count, each preset count reached is used to control outputs: each step relates to a certain output or group of outputs. The outputs are internal relays, which in turn control the external output devices. The step pulses come from a timer (time-driven) or from sensors (event-driven). Many PLCs provide a sequencer instruction (Allen-Bradley SQO, Siemens DRUM) that steps through a table of output words; the ladder below shows the principle with a counter and comparisons.

Rung 3: tin pulse · deflector off → C1 counts tins sent to the 6-tin box.

2023 · Q7(a)Write short notes on drum sequencer with necessary diagram.10Topic: drum sequencer

Drum sequencer. The drum sequencer is a form of counter used for sequential control of machines with a stepped sequence of repeatable operations (washing machines, packaging, traffic lights). It replaces the mechanical drum sequencer — a drum with protruding pegs (Fig. 7.4): as the drum rotates step by step, each peg closes the contact aligned with it while it passes, so each row of pegs switches one output on at the programmed steps.

In a PLC the drum is a master counter whose count is the step number. The step input comes from a timer (time-driven sequence) or from sensors (event-driven). At each preset count reached, a pattern of outputs is switched on: each step relates to an output or a group of outputs, which are internal relays that in turn drive the external devices. The pattern is a step–output table (the electronic “pegs”).

Example (lecture slide 9): output 1 on from 5 s to 10 s, output 2 from 10 s to 20 s, output 3 from 15 s to 25 s, output 4 from 25 s to 30 s. With 5 s steps:

Step (count)Time (s)Out 1Out 2Out 3Out 4
00–50000
15–101000
210–150100
315–200110
420–250010
525–300001

Advantages: one instruction/table replaces many timers and rungs; the sequence is changed by editing the table; easy to monitor (the step number shows where the machine is). Limitation: a purely time-driven drum does not check that each operation actually finished — event-driven steps or watchdog timers (§10.5) are added for that.

8. Shift Registers ★★★

8.1 Registers and Shift Registers

Definitions (lecture)
A register is an electronic device in which data can be stored; in a PLC it is a number of internal relays grouped together, normally 8, 16 or 32. Each relay is effectively open or closed, designated 0 or 1 — one bit. A shift register is a number of internal relays grouped together which allow the stored bits to be shifted from one relay to the next — like a group of flip-flops connected in series that store and shift bits left or right with clock pulses.

A shift register needs three inputs:

  1. Data (OUT) — the bit to be loaded into the first location;
  2. Shift (SFT) — the command (clock pulse) that moves every bit along by one location;
  3. Reset (RST) — clears the register to all zeros.

The grouping of internal relays into a shift register is done automatically by the PLC when the shift-register function is selected. In Mitsubishi PLCs the code SFT is used against the internal relay that is the first in the array (e.g. M140), and a block of relays from that number (M140–M157) is reserved. Siemens provides word instructions SHL_W (shift left a word) and SHR_W (shift right) with inputs EN, IN (word), N (number of places) and output OUT; S7-1200 SHL/SHR work the same way. A bit-shift such as Allen-Bradley BSL/BSR loads a data bit and shifts on each rising edge of its enable — the form used in this chapter.

8.2 Ladder Programs

The register outputs are used as contacts like any internal relays. Each shift pulse moves the pattern one relay along, so a single 1 loaded at the start walks through the outputs one at a time — a simple sequencer. A pattern of 1s and 0s that moves with a conveyor tracks items.

Lecture application 1 — sequencing (cylinders A and B, sequence A+, B+, A−, B−): the Start input loads a 1 into IR1 (register 1000). Each limit switch (a+, b+, a−) gives a pulse that shifts the register: a+ gives 0100 (IR2 → B+), b+ gives 0010 (IR3 → A−), a− gives 0001 (IR4 → B−), b− gives 0000; the register outputs IR1–IR4 drive the valve solenoids A+, B+, A−, B−.

Lecture application 2 — keeping track of items (rejecting faulty items): a sensor X400 detects a faulty item and loads 1 into M140; each movement of the conveyor by one item pitch (X401) shifts the register; when the faulty item reaches the rejection point, four positions later, M144 = 1 and activates the reject mechanism Y430 (through a reset latch M100 so that it acts once per item).

8.3 Solved Past Questions

2022 · Q8(b)Define shift register. How this can be represented in ladder diagram? Explain with an example of 4-bit shift register.11Topic: shift register in ladder form

Definition. A shift register is a group of internal relays (bits) — usually 8, 16 or 32 — that store binary data and allow the stored bits to be shifted from one relay to the next each time a shift pulse is received; the bit at the input enters the first location and the last bit overflows (Fig. 8.1).

Representation in ladder. A shift register is shown either as three special coils — OUT (data input), SFT (shift) and RST (reset) — all addressed to the first relay of the register (Mitsubishi, Fig. 8.2), or as a single box (Siemens SHL/SHR, A-B BSL) with a data input, an enable (shift) input and the register address. The register bits are then used as contacts in the following rungs to drive outputs.

Example — 4-bit shift register (Siemens addressing):

Given Data
Data input I0.0; shift pulse I0.1 (rising edge); reset I0.2; register bits M10.0–M10.3 (bit 1–bit 4); outputs Q0.0–Q0.3.

Operation. At each rising edge of the shift input: bit 4 ← bit 3, bit 3 ← bit 2, bit 2 ← bit 1, bit 1 ← data input; the old bit 4 is lost. Outputs Q0.0–Q0.3 follow bits 1–4.

Given Data (allocation and assumed times)
Start I0.0, Stop I0.1, bottle-height sensor I0.2 (1 = 500 mL bottle at the sensor), index sensor I0.3 (one pulse per conveyor step). Conveyor motor Q0.0; filling valves of nozzles 1–6: Q0.1–Q0.6. Step 1 — tracking (rung 3). Each index pulse (rising edge of I0.3) shifts SR1 by one place and loads the height-sensor state of the bottle arriving from the sensor position into M10.0. So after every step, M10.k holds the size of the bottle under nozzle k+1. The same pulse counts the step in C1.

Step 2 — six bottles in place (rung 4). After 6 steps C1 is done: all six nozzle positions hold bottles → SET “filling” M0.1, which stops the conveyor (rung 2).

Step 3 — timers (rungs 5–7). Filling starts T1 (4 s) and T2 (8 s) together. M0.2 = filling · NOT T1 (250 mL window); M0.3 = filling · NOT T2 (500 mL window).

Step 4 — nozzles (rungs 8–13). Valve k = (M10.k · M0.3) + (NOT M10.k · M0.2): a nozzle over a 500 mL bottle is open for 8 s, over a 250 mL bottle for 4 s.

Step 5 — release (rung 14). When T2 is done all bottles are full: reset M0.1 and C1; the conveyor restarts, moves the filled bottles out and brings the next six, while the shift register keeps tracking.

Check (simulation with random bottles): the first batch was 250, 250, 500, 500, 250, 250 mL under nozzles 1–6 and the valve-open times were 4, 4, 8, 8, 4, 4 s — every nozzle filled its own bottle size.

Shift on each index pulse; fill after 6 steps: 500 mL → 8 s, 250 mL → 4 s

Assumptions
Bottles are fed one per conveyor step with no gaps (the question says six bottles are in the filler). The fill times are not given and are assumed; in practice they are set from the valve flow rate (e.g. 62.5 mL/s gives 4 s and 8 s).
