9. Data Handling ★★★

9.1 Data in a PLC

Definition (lecture)
Data handling consists of operations involving moving or transferring numeric information stored in one memory word location to another word in a different location, comparing data values, and carrying out simple arithmetic operations. For example, a numeric value may need to be compared with a set value and an action initiated if the actual value is less than the set value.

Bits are grouped into words (16 bits, e.g. MW10 = bytes MB10 and MB11) or double words (32 bits, MD20). Words hold integers (−32 768 … 32 767), timer and counter values, analog input readings (IW64 on S7-1200, 0–27 648 for 0–10 V), set-points and calculation results. BCD (binary-coded decimal) represents each decimal digit by 4 bits (123 → 0001 0010 0011); it is used with thumbwheel switches and 7-segment displays, and conversion instructions (BCD → binary, binary → BCD) are provided.

9.2 Data Movement

A move copies a value from a source address to a destination address when the rung is true; the source is unchanged. Typically one rung is used for each move. Formats (lecture Fig. 12.2): Mitsubishi MOV S D (source D1, destination D2); Allen-Bradley MOV N7:0 N7:2; Siemens MOVE box with EN/ENO, IN and OUT (some Siemens PLCs treat it as “load into the accumulator, then transfer”). In structured text: Result := value;.

Typical moves: a preset value to a timer or counter (N7:0 → T4:6.PRE) to change a recipe time; a counter’s accumulated value to a register for storage or display (C5:18.ACC → N7:0); an input word to a register (I:012 → N7:0, reading a thumbwheel or analog value); a register to an output word (N7:0 → O:030, driving a display). Block moves (BLKMOV, MOVE_BLK) copy whole tables, and FILL writes one value into many words.

9.3 Data Comparison

A comparison instruction compares two data values and gives a 1 (true) or 0 (false) result that acts like a contact in the rung. The usual comparisons are: equal (= , ==, EQ, EQU); not equal (<>, NE, NEQ); greater than (>, GT, GRT); greater than or equal (>=, GE, GEQ); less than (<, LT, LES); less than or equal (<=, LE, LEQ); and in S7-1200 also IN_RANGE and OUT_RANGE. Formats (lecture Fig. 12.4): Mitsubishi [> S D]; Allen-Bradley GRT T4.0.ACC 400; Siemens CMP>R with IN1, IN2 (R = real, I = 16-bit integer, D = 32-bit integer; both inputs of the same type). Structured text: Output := P2 < P1;.

9.4 Data Selection

Selection instructions choose one of several data values to pass on, according to a selector input or to their size (IEC 61131-3 selection functions):

  • SEL — binary selection: OUT = IN0 if G = 0, OUT = IN1 if G = 1 (e.g. choose the summer or winter set-point with a selector switch).
  • MUX — multiplexer: OUT = INK, the input whose number is given by K (e.g. recipe 0–7 chosen from an HMI).
  • MAX / MIN — the largest / smallest of the inputs (e.g. the hottest of several zones).
  • LIMIT — OUT = IN clamped between MN and MX (e.g. keep a speed set-point within 0–1500 rpm).

Selection is also done with comparisons and moves: if a condition is true, MOVE value A to the destination, otherwise MOVE value B.

9.5 Arithmetic Functions and Closed-Loop Control

PLCs provide ADD, SUB, MUL, DIV (Siemens ADD box with EN, IN1, IN2, OUT; Allen-Bradley CPT computes an expression into a destination), increment/decrement, and conversions (BCD_I, I_BCD, scaling NORM_X/SCALE_X). Uses: counting totals, scaling analog values to engineering units, computing averages and set-point errors.

In closed-loop control the PLC reads the measured value through an ADC, compares it with the set value, and drives the actuator through a DAC so as to reduce the error. Modes of control: on–off (two-step, with a hysteresis band — §9.6 Q2), proportional (output ∝ error), integral (output ∝ integral of the error, removes offset) and derivative (output ∝ rate of change). The IEC PID block has inputs AUTO, PV (process variable), SP (set point), X0, KP, TR (integral time), TD (derivative time) and CYCLE, and output XOUT.

9.6 Solved Past Questions

2022 · Q8(c)Discuss data movement, data comparison, and data selection process for PLC.12Topic: data movement, comparison and selection

Data handling covers instructions that work on whole words of data (numbers) rather than single bits: moving, comparing, selecting and arithmetic.

1. Data movement. A MOVE instruction copies the data in a source word to a destination word when the rung is true; the source keeps its value. Each move normally has its own rung. Examples: Mitsubishi MOV D1 D2; Allen-Bradley MOV N7:0 N7:2; Siemens MOVE box (EN, IN → OUT) (Fig. 9.1). Applications: loading a new preset into a timer or counter (N7:0 → T4:6.PRE), storing a counter’s accumulated value (C5:18.ACC → N7:0), reading an input word or analog value into a register (I:012 → N7:0), and sending a register to an output word or display (N7:0 → O:030).

2. Data comparison. A compare instruction tests two values — e.g. a sensor reading against a set value held in a register — for =, ≠, >, ≥, <, ≤, and gives a true/false result that acts as a contact controlling the rest of the rung. Examples: Mitsubishi [> S D]; Allen-Bradley GRT T4.0.ACC 400; Siemens CMP>I IN1 IN2. Applications: an alarm set when the temperature reaches 100 °C and reset below 90 °C (Fig. 9.2); switching several outputs in sequence with a single timer by comparing its elapsed time with 5 s, 15 s, … (Fig. 9.3); pump control between two levels (Q2 below).

3. Data selection. Selection instructions pass one of several values to an output: SEL (G = 0 → IN0, G = 1 → IN1), MUX (choose input K of many), MAX/MIN (largest/smallest value), LIMIT (clamp a value between a minimum and a maximum). Example: a selector switch I0.2 chooses between two recipe temperatures MW50 and MW52, and the selected value goes to the set-point MW54 (Fig. 9.1, SEL rung). Without a SEL block the same is done by two MOVE rungs, one enabled by I0.2 and the other by NOT I0.2.

Process. In each scan the CPU executes these boxes in rung order: a box executes only when power reaches EN, reads its input words from memory, performs the operation in the ALU, and writes the result word (or the 1/0 result for a comparison) back to memory, where the following rungs can use it.

10. Safe Systems, Commissioning and Fault Finding SUPPLEMENTARY ★★★

These topics are asked in 2023 and 2024 but are not on the lecture slides; the chapter follows W. Bolton, Programmable Logic Controllers, Ch. 13 (Designing systems), and standard practice.

10.1 Safe Systems

Safety legislation requires employers to make the workplace safe: to assess the risks (identify hazards, who may be harmed and how, how likely harm is, whether existing precautions are enough), to record the findings and to review them. Emergency stops, guards and access doors are designed from this assessment — e.g. switch contacts on access doors stop the machine if a door is not correctly guarding it. The key standard is IEC 61508, Functional safety of electrical/electronic/programmable electronic safety-related systems (seven parts: general requirements, E/E/PE system requirements, software, definitions, safety integrity levels, guidelines, techniques). For functional safety the safety-related system must work correctly and, when a failure occurs, bring the plant to a safe shut-down state (machinery: ISO 13849, IEC 62061, IEC 60204-1 for E-stops).

10.2 PLC Systems and Safety

Design rule
Emergency stop buttons and safety-guard switches must be hard-wired and must not depend on the PLC software, so that if the stop switch or the PLC fails the system is automatically safe — the system must be fail-safe.

Putting the emergency stop only in the PLC input is unsafe, because it then depends on the PLC working. The safer arrangement puts the emergency-stop switch hard-wired in the output circuit (Fig. 10.2): pressing it de-energises the motor contactor directly. When it is released the motor does not restart, because the internal relay latch in the PLC has already dropped out (the contactor feedback or the latch prevents automatic restart).

10.3 Emergency-Stop Relays and Safety Relays

Emergency-stop (safety) relays, e.g. the Pilz PNOZ, are special relays that monitor the E-stop circuit independently of the PLC. They have LEDs showing the state of the input and output circuits, the reset circuit, the supply and faults, and an interface (opto-isolated) through which a PLC can read their status — so the PLC can start a safe close-down sequence, while the stop itself does not depend on the PLC.

Safety is increased further with three contacts in series (one NC and two NO, so one relay must be de-energised and two energised), with monitored reset (the relay restarts only after a deliberate reset with the E-stop released) and with a feedback loop through NC auxiliary contacts of the contactors (the relay will not reset if a contactor has welded). Stop relays are combined with light curtains (infrared beams round a danger zone — breaking a beam triggers a safe shutdown), safety mats (stepping on the mat closes a contact) and interlocked guards. Safety PLCs (e.g. SIMATIC S5-95F) contain two or three processors running the same program, comparing inputs, outputs and intermediate results, and go to a safe stop on any disagreement; either channel alone can switch the outputs off.

10.4 Commissioning

Commissioning of a PLC system involves (Bolton §13.3):

  1. checking that all cable connections between the PLC and the plant are complete, safe, to the required specification and meet local standards;
  2. checking that the incoming power supply matches the voltage setting of the PLC;
  3. checking that all protective devices are set to their correct trip settings;
  4. checking that the emergency stop buttons work;
  5. checking that all input/output devices are connected to the correct I/O points and give the correct signals;
  6. loading and testing the software.

Testing inputs and outputs. Each input device is operated and the input LED on the module is watched: it should be on when the input is closed and off when open. If not, the input device, its wiring, its supply, or the LED/input module is at fault. Outputs that can be safely started are tested with push buttons or by forcing.

Forcing means switching inputs or outputs on or off by software from the programming terminal instead of by the real devices: the PLC is put in force/monitor mode, the address is entered (e.g. FORCE Y005 → “Y005 fON”; FORCE X001 → “X001 fOFF”), and the forced state overrides the real one. A forced input checks that the program responds; a forced output checks the output channel, wiring and actuator.

Testing software. The PLC’s checking program lists the I/O points used, timer and counter settings and errors such as an output used twice, a timer or counter without a preset, or a counter without a reset. Simulation (monitor/test/debug mode) writes directly into the I/O memory so the program can be run with simulated inputs and the preset values checked; the screen shows open/closed contacts and energised coils as the program runs.

10.5 Fault Finding and Fault-Detection Techniques

In a PLC-controlled plant most faults are in the sensors, actuators and wiring, not in the PLC; within the PLC most are in the I/O channels or power supply rather than the CPU. Examples: an output LED on but the device not working → check the voltage at the output terminal (normal) and at the device (absent → wiring fault; present → device fault); all inputs failing → a short or earth fault on one input, found by disconnecting inputs one by one; the whole system stopped → power failure, supply switched off or a breaker tripped. PLCs also have built-in self-tests that display fault codes with recovery actions.

Fault-detection techniques:

  1. Timing checks (watchdog). A watchdog timer checks that a function is completed within its normal time; if not, a fault is assumed, an alarm is set and the system may be shut down. Internally, the PLC’s watchdog is preset slightly longer than the normal scan time, restarted every scan, and trips if a scan takes too long. In the user program, a timer is started when a function starts; if the function finishes first the program continues, otherwise a jump goes to fault rungs (alarm, stop).
  2. Last output set. Status lamps (or HMI indicators) show the last output that was set in a sequence that has halted; each new output turns its lamp on and the previous lamps off, so the halted step is identified. For large systems the outputs are grouped, one lamp per group, with a selector switch to pick the output within the group.
  3. Replication. Operations are duplicated — the program repeats each operation twice, or two PLCs run in parallel — and the results compared; a difference shows a (possibly transient) fault.
  4. Expected-value checks. Software errors are detected by checking that a specific input gives the expected value; if not, a fault is assumed.

Program storage. Programs in battery-backed RAM are lost if the battery fails, so EPROM/flash storage and a back-up copy of every program (CD, hard disk, memory card) are kept, so the program can be reloaded without rewriting.

10.6 Solved Past Questions

2024 · Q6(a)Draw and explain a typical emergency stop relay wiring diagram.10Topic: emergency-stop relay wiring

Diagram: draw Fig. 10.3 (both modes), or the complete safety-relay connection of Fig. 10.4.

Explanation.

  1. Purpose: the emergency stop must act independently of the PLC and be fail-safe, so it is wired to a dedicated emergency-stop (safety) relay that switches the power to the hazardous loads directly. The PLC only reads the relay’s status.
  2. Input circuit: the E-stop is a red mushroom-head push button with normally closed contacts, so the relay is energised only while the button is not pressed and the wiring is intact. Pressing the button — or a broken wire, or loss of supply — de-energises the relay: the stop works in every failure of the input circuit.
  3. Single-channel mode (Fig. 10.3a): one NC contact in the coil circuit of one relay K1; the K1 contact supplies the motor contactor. Weakness: if the K1 contact welds, pressing the E-stop does not stop the motor.
  4. Dual-channel mode (Fig. 10.3b): the E-stop has two NC contacts feeding two channels (K1 and K2), and the K1 and K2 output contacts are in series in the load circuit: one welded contact cannot prevent the stop. A cross-fault between channels is detected by the relay.
  5. Monitored reset (S33/S34): after an emergency stop the outputs come back only when the E-stop is released and the reset button is pressed deliberately; the relay checks the reset button too (a jammed reset does not restart the machine).
  6. Feedback loop (Y1/Y2): NC auxiliary contacts of the output contactors K3/K4 are wired in series to the relay; it can reset only if both contactors have really dropped out (no welded main contacts).
  7. Status output (e.g. Y32): an auxiliary output, opto-isolated, goes to a PLC input so the PLC knows an emergency stop occurred and can run a safe shutdown sequence and display the fault; it is not part of the safety path.
Source lecturePriyo Sir · Textbook – W. Bolton, PLCs, 4th ed. (Programmable Logic Controllers 4th Edition (W Bolton).pdf, pp. 226–229) — not on the slides — from the reference textbook
2023 · Q8(a)How can safety relays improve system safety and ensure prompt shutdown in case of failures? Explain with necessary circuit diagram.10Topic: safety relays

Circuit diagram: Fig. 10.4 (dual-channel E-stop, safety relay, redundant contactors with feedback, PLC status input), supported by Fig. 10.3.

How safety relays improve safety:

  1. Independent of the PLC. The stop function is hard-wired through the safety relay, so a PLC hardware or software fault cannot prevent a stop. The PLC receives only a status signal (opto-isolated interface) to start a controlled close-down.
  2. Fail-safe (de-energise to trip). The safety relay is energised in normal operation through the NC contacts of E-stops, guard switches, light curtains or safety mats. Any demand or any failure — broken wire, lost supply, loose terminal — de-energises it and switches off the load. Shutdown is therefore prompt: the hazardous energy is cut by relay contacts in milliseconds, without waiting for a PLC scan.
  3. Redundancy. Two (or three) channels and force-guided contacts in series: a single welded contact or a single failed relay cannot keep the machine running.
  4. Self-monitoring. The relay checks its own contacts at every cycle, detects cross-faults between the channels and short circuits, and refuses to reset if a fault is present.
  5. Feedback monitoring of the contactors (Y1–Y2 loop): a welded contactor is detected, because the relay will not reset until both contactors have dropped out.
  6. Monitored manual reset: the machine does not restart by itself when the E-stop is released or power returns; a deliberate reset is needed.
  7. Integration of other safety devices: light curtains round a danger zone, interlocked guards and safety mats are connected to the same relay inputs, giving a complete safe work cell; for complex machines a safety PLC (two processors cross-checking) performs the same role.
Source lecturePriyo Sir · Textbook – W. Bolton, PLCs, 4th ed. (Programmable Logic Controllers 4th Edition (W Bolton).pdf, pp. 226–229) — not on the slides — from the reference textbook
2023 · Q8(b)Describe briefly the timing checks and last output set fault detection techniques.10Topic: watchdog and last-output-set diagnostics

1. Timing checks (watchdog timers). A watchdog checks that a function is completed within its normal time; if it is not, a fault is assumed, an alarm is given and the system may be shut down.

  • Inside the PLC: the internal watchdog is preset slightly longer than the normal scan time, restarted at the beginning of each scan and reset at its end. If a scan takes too long (endless loop, hardware fault) it times out and the PLC goes to STOP with a fault indication.
  • In the user program: a timer is started when a movement starts. Example (Fig. 10.6): Start energises the solenoid valve Q0.0 so the piston extends, and starts T1 (5 s; normal stroke ≈ 3 s). When the piston is fully extended its limit switch I0.1 stops the timer. If the limit switch is not reached within 5 s (sticking piston, failed valve or sensor) T1 times out, sets the alarm Q0.1, switches off the solenoid and jumps to the fault routine.

2. Last output set. Status lamps show which output was set last in a sequence that has stopped, so the point of failure is found immediately. The program is arranged so that each new output turns on its own status lamp and turns off the previous ones.

In Fig. 10.7, when output 0 comes on, M5.0 is set and lamp 0 lights; when output 1 comes on, M5.1 is set, M5.0 reset, and lamp 1 lights. If the machine stops, the lit lamp shows the last step reached (simulated). In a large system the outputs are grouped with one lamp per group and a selector switch picks the output within the group, to avoid a lamp for every output.

2023 · Q8(c)Explain how using forcing, the failure of an input sensor or its wiring can be detected.10Topic: forcing for fault diagnosis

Forcing means setting an input or output on or off from the programming terminal by software, overriding its real state (the PLC is put in force/monitor mode; e.g. keys FORCE X001 ENTER, answer YES/NO → display “X001 fON”).

Procedure (Fig. 10.8):

  1. Operate the sensor physically (place the target, press the switch) and watch the input LED on the PLC module (and the input bit in monitor mode). If the LED comes on, the sensor and its wiring are working.
  2. If the LED does not come on, the fault may be in the sensor, its wiring, its power supply, or the PLC input channel/LED.
  3. Force that input ON from the terminal. If the input LED/bit now comes on and the program responds correctly (the expected output switches), the PLC input channel and the program are good — so the fault must be in the sensor or its wiring (or the sensor supply).
  4. If forcing does not produce the response, the fault is in the input module/LED or in the program.
  5. Distinguish sensor from wiring with a meter: measure the voltage at the PLC input terminal while operating the sensor. 0 V at the terminal but the correct voltage at the sensor output → broken wiring; no voltage at the sensor output with its supply present → faulty sensor.
Safety when forcing
Forcing operates the plant without the real interlocks — make sure forced outputs cannot hurt anyone, and remove all forces after testing (many PLCs show a “FORCE” LED while any force is active).
Source lecturePriyo Sir · Textbook – W. Bolton, PLCs, 4th ed. (Programmable Logic Controllers 4th Edition (W Bolton).pdf, pp. 229–231) — not on the slides — from the reference textbook
2024 · Q6(b)Explain how the failure of an input sensor or its wiring can be detected using forcing?10Topic: forcing for fault diagnosis

This is the 2023 Q8(c) question in different words; the full answer and flowchart are above (Fig. 10.8). Summary for the exam:

  1. Forcing = turning an input or output on/off from the programming terminal by software (force/monitor mode), independent of the real device.
  2. Operate the sensor and observe the input LED. LED on → sensor and wiring OK.
  3. LED off → force the input ON. If the PLC now sees the input (LED/bit on) and the program gives the correct output, the input channel and program are healthy, so the failure is in the sensor or its wiring. If forcing gives no response, the input module or the program is at fault.
  4. Locate it: with the sensor operated, measure the voltage at the input terminal and at the sensor output — voltage at the sensor but not at the terminal → wiring (open circuit, loose terminal); no voltage at the sensor output although it is supplied → sensor faulty.
  5. Remove the force after the test.
Source lecturePriyo Sir · Textbook – W. Bolton, PLCs, 4th ed. (Programmable Logic Controllers 4th Edition (W Bolton).pdf, pp. 229–231) — not on the slides — from the reference textbook
2023 · Q8(d)What are the steps in commissioning of a PLC system?05Topic: commissioning

Commissioning of a PLC system involves (Fig. 10.5):

  1. Checking that all cable connections between the PLC and the plant are complete, safe, to specification and to local standards.
  2. Checking that the incoming power supply matches the voltage setting of the PLC.
  3. Checking that all protective devices are set to their correct trip settings.
  4. Checking that the emergency stop buttons work.
  5. Checking that all input/output devices are connected to the correct I/O points and give the correct signals (operate inputs and watch the LEDs; test outputs by push buttons or forcing).
  6. Loading and testing the software — software check for address errors, simulation/monitor mode, then trial runs of the complete system.
